claim: Avoiding distraction by salient yet irrelevant stimuli is critical when accomplishing daily tasks.
source: Avoiding distraction by salient yet irrelevant stimuli is critical when accomplishing daily tasks.
evidence: This is a general statement about cognitive function that draws from established understanding in cognitive psychology and neuroscience.

claim: The behavioral benefits of distractor suppression are well established.
source: While the behavioral benefits of distractor suppression are well established, its neural underpinnings are not yet fully understood.
evidence: This statement references established scientific consensus in the field of attention research.

claim: The neural underpinnings of distractor suppression are not yet fully understood.
source: While the behavioral benefits of distractor suppression are well established, its neural underpinnings are not yet fully understood.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current scientific knowledge.

claim: Implicit spatial priors shape sensory processing at the earliest stages of cortical visual processing in early visual cortex.
source: Our findings indicate that implicit spatial priors shape sensory processing even at the earliest stages of cortical visual processing, evident in early visual cortex as a suppression of stimuli at locations which frequently contained distracting information.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fMRI data presented in the study showing BOLD response modulations in early visual cortex.

claim: Suppression in early visual cortex is evident as reduced responses to stimuli at locations which frequently contained distracting information.
source: Our findings indicate that implicit spatial priors shape sensory processing even at the earliest stages of cortical visual processing, evident in early visual cortex as a suppression of stimuli at locations which frequently contained distracting information.
evidence: This is directly supported by the fMRI BOLD response data showing reduced activation at high-probability distractor locations.

claim: Neural suppression in early visual cortex is spatially (receptive field) specific.
source: Notably, while this suppression was spatially (receptive field) specific, it did extend to nearby neutral locations and occurred regardless of whether distractors, nontarget items, or targets were presented at this location, suggesting that suppression arises before stimulus identification.
evidence: This is supported by the ROI-based fMRI analysis showing location-specific BOLD modulations.

claim: Neural suppression extends to nearby neutral locations.
source: Notably, while this suppression was spatially (receptive field) specific, it did extend to nearby neutral locations and occurred regardless of whether distractors, nontarget items, or targets were presented at this location, suggesting that suppression arises before stimulus identification.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fMRI data showing suppression at NL-near locations in addition to HPDL.

claim: Neural suppression occurs regardless of whether distractors, nontarget items, or targets were presented at the suppressed location.
source: Notably, while this suppression was spatially (receptive field) specific, it did extend to nearby neutral locations and occurred regardless of whether distractors, nontarget items, or targets were presented at this location, suggesting that suppression arises before stimulus identification.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data showing similar suppression patterns across all stimulus types at HPDL and NL-near locations.

claim: Suppression arises before stimulus identification.
source: Notably, while this suppression was spatially (receptive field) specific, it did extend to nearby neutral locations and occurred regardless of whether distractors, nontarget items, or targets were presented at this location, suggesting that suppression arises before stimulus identification.
evidence: This is inferred from the stimulus-unspecific nature of the suppression observed in the fMRI data.

claim: Spatially specific neural suppression occurs even when search is only anticipated but no search display is presented.
source: Crucially, we observed similar spatially specific neural suppression even if search was only anticipated, but no search display was presented.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data from omission trials showing location-specific BOLD suppression.

claim: The brain leverages implicitly learned prior knowledge to optimize sensory processing and attention allocation.
source: Combined, our study underscores how the brain leverages implicitly learned prior knowledge to optimize sensory processing and attention allocation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the behavioral and neural data presented in the study.

claim: Selective attention enables us to navigate complex settings and perform challenging tasks.
source: Selective attention is pivotal in our daily interactions with the environment, enabling us to navigate complex settings and perform challenging tasks.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge in cognitive psychology about the role of selective attention.

claim: Suppression of nonessential stimuli is essential for maintaining focus on critical activities.
source: Essential for this capability is the suppression of nonessential stimuli allowing us to maintain focus on critical activities, like driving a car, by filtering out salient yet irrelevant information that could otherwise divert our attention.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of attentional mechanisms in cognitive science.

claim: The behavioral advantages of distractor suppression have been extensively documented.
source: The behavioral advantages of distractor suppression have been extensively documented, underscoring its significance in enhancing cognitive efficiency and task performance (Chelazzi et al., 2019; Luck et al., 2021; Theeuwes et al., 2022; van Moorselaar and Slagter, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research in the field.

claim: Distractor suppression enhances cognitive efficiency and task performance.
source: The behavioral advantages of distractor suppression have been extensively documented, underscoring its significance in enhancing cognitive efficiency and task performance (Chelazzi et al., 2019; Luck et al., 2021; Theeuwes et al., 2022; van Moorselaar and Slagter, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Traditional models of attention posit that the visual system prioritizes relevant stimuli while suppressing irrelevant ones.
source: Traditional models of attention posit that the visual system is adept at prioritizing relevant stimuli while suppressing irrelevant ones, a process facilitated by both bottom-up (stimulus-driven) and top-down (goal-directed) mechanisms (Awh et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement describes established theoretical models in attention research, supported by citation.

claim: Attention is facilitated by both bottom-up (stimulus-driven) and top-down (goal-directed) mechanisms.
source: Traditional models of attention posit that the visual system is adept at prioritizing relevant stimuli while suppressing irrelevant ones, a process facilitated by both bottom-up (stimulus-driven) and top-down (goal-directed) mechanisms (Awh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established attention research.

claim: Recent advancements suggest a more nuanced understanding of attention, incorporating the role of prior knowledge derived by statistical learning.
source: Yet, recent advancements suggest a more nuanced understanding, incorporating the role of prior knowledge derived by statistical learning (Theeuwes et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: Salient distractors result in less behavioral interference if they appear at locations with higher probability.
source: Indeed, salient distractors result in less behavioral interference if they appear at locations with higher probability, showing that implicitly learned prior knowledge can aid distractor suppression (Ferrante et al., 2018; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018a; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: Implicitly learned prior knowledge can aid distractor suppression.
source: Indeed, salient distractors result in less behavioral interference if they appear at locations with higher probability, showing that implicitly learned prior knowledge can aid distractor suppression (Ferrante et al., 2018; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018a; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The visual system shows sensitivity to statistical regularity, including suppressed neural responses to predicted compared to surprising stimuli through the visual hierarchy.
source: The visual system shows a remarkable sensitivity to statistical regularity, including suppressed neural responses to predicted compared to surprising stimuli through the visual hierarchy (Melloni et al., 2012; Richter et al., 2018; Richter and de Lange, 2019; Won et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: The visual system is likely to play a role in facilitating distractor suppression using acquired prior knowledge.
source: Therefore, the visual system is likely to play a role in facilitating distractor suppression using acquired prior knowledge, attenuating neural responses to predictable distractors possibly already at the first stages of the visual cortical hierarchy, in early visual cortex (EVC; primary and second visual cortex).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from previous findings about statistical learning in the visual system.

claim: Statistical regularities during visual search modulate neural processing in early visual cortex.
source: Indeed, in line with this proposition, recent functional MRI (fMRI) work suggests that statistical regularities during visual search modulate neural processing in EVC (Adam and Serences, 2021; Beffara et al., 2023; Won et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent fMRI studies.

claim: BOLD responses in early visual cortex are enhanced when targets appear at predictable locations.
source: Specifically, BOLD responses, including in EVC, are enhanced when targets (Beffara et al., 2023) or suppressed when distractors (Zhang et al., 2022) appear at predictable locations.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: BOLD responses in early visual cortex are suppressed when distractors appear at predictable locations.
source: Specifically, BOLD responses, including in EVC, are enhanced when targets (Beffara et al., 2023) or suppressed when distractors (Zhang et al., 2022) appear at predictable locations.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Findings are consistent with the notion of spatial priority maps facilitating visual search by both target enhancement and distractor suppression.
source: Together these findings are consistent with the notion of spatial priority maps, reflecting prior knowledge, facilitating visual search by both target enhancement and distractor suppression (Awh et al., 2012; Bisley and Goldberg, 2010; Fecteau and Munoz, 2006; Itti and Koch, 2000; Serences and Yantis, 2006; Theeuwes et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings supported by citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: It is unknown how spatially specific distractor suppression is in early visual cortex.
source: It is at present unknown how spatially specific distractor suppression is, as previous studies using fMRI utilized paradigms in which entire regions were likely to contain distractors (Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge based on limitations of previous studies.

claim: Learned suppression at the behavioral level is often characterized by a gradient around the high-probability distractor location.
source: This leaves open the question whether learned suppression in EVC, which at the behavioral level is often characterized by a gradient around the high-probability distractor location (HPDL) (Wang and Theeuwes, 2018a), is spatially specific or alternatively more widespread.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a behavioral study.

claim: It is unclear whether suppression in early visual cortex is stimulus-specific or stimulus-unspecific.
source: Moreover, it is unclear whether suppression in EVC is stimulus-specific, affecting only distractors, or stimulus-unspecific as proposed by a recent study (Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This identifies an open question in the field, referencing a previous study.

claim: It is contested whether spatial priority maps underlying distractor suppression are deployed proactively or reactively.
source: Finally, it is widely contested whether spatial priority maps underlying distractor suppression are deployed proactively (i.e. predictively before stimulus onset), as suggested by some accounts (Huang et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2022), or reactively following visual search onset (Chang et al., 2023; Moher and Egeth, 2012).
evidence: This describes an ongoing debate in the field, supported by citations to conflicting studies.

claim: Early visual cortex is sensitive to spatial statistical regularities.
source: To foreshadow the results, data show that EVC is sensitive to spatial statistical regularities, evident as a suppression of neural responses corresponding to locations that frequently contained distracting stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by the fMRI data presented in the study.

claim: Neural suppression in early visual cortex is broad, encompassing nearby neutral locations.
source: However, this suppression was surprisingly broad, encompassing nearby neutral locations.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data showing suppression at NL-near locations.

claim: Neural suppression emerges proactively in conditions where search display is expected but not presented.
source: Critically, we also demonstrate that this suppression emerges proactively, in conditions in which the search display is expected but not actually presented (omission trials).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data from omission trials.

claim: Participants were exposed to an additional singleton task where one location more frequently contained a salient distractor.
source: Participants were exposed to an additional singleton task where, unbeknownst to them, one location more frequently contained a salient distractor.
evidence: This describes the experimental design used in the study.

claim: Participants were unaware that one location more frequently contained a salient distractor.
source: Participants were exposed to an additional singleton task where, unbeknownst to them, one location more frequently contained a salient distractor.
evidence: This describes a key aspect of the experimental design to ensure implicit learning.

claim: RTs were fastest when no distractor was present (833 ms).
source: RTs were fastest when no distractor was present (833 ms; post hoc tests: Absent vs NL-far: t(27) = 4.27, pholm<0.001, d=0.31; Absent vs NL-near: t(27) = 4.49, pholm<0.001, d=0.33; Absent vs HPDL t(27) = 1.70, pholm = 0.188, d=0.12; BF10=1.90).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral RT data.

claim: For trials containing a distractor, the fastest RTs were observed for distractor stimuli appearing at the HPDL (848 ms).
source: For trials containing a distractor, the fastest RTs were observed for distractor stimuli appearing at the HPDL (848 ms; HPDL vs NL-far: t(27) = 2.57, pholm = 0.036, d=0.19; HPDL vs NL-near: t(27) = 2.79, pholm = 0.026, d=0.20), showing clear evidence of behavioral facilitation due to learning of the statistical regularities governing distractor appearances.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral RT data.

claim: Behavioral data show clear evidence of behavioral facilitation due to learning of the statistical regularities governing distractor appearances.
source: For trials containing a distractor, the fastest RTs were observed for distractor stimuli appearing at the HPDL (848 ms; HPDL vs NL-far: t(27) = 2.57, pholm = 0.036, d=0.19; HPDL vs NL-near: t(27) = 2.79, pholm = 0.026, d=0.20), showing clear evidence of behavioral facilitation due to learning of the statistical regularities governing distractor appearances.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral RT data showing faster responses at HPDL.

claim: Responses were similarly slow at the near neutral (871 ms) and far neutral locations (870 ms).
source: Responses were similarly slow at the near neutral (871 ms) and far neutral locations (870 ms; NL-far vs NL-near: t(27) = 0.22, pholm = 0.828, d=0.02; BF10=0.20), highlighting the spatial specificity of learned suppression.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral RT data.

claim: The similarity of RTs at near and far neutral locations highlights the spatial specificity of learned suppression.
source: Responses were similarly slow at the near neutral (871 ms) and far neutral locations (870 ms; NL-far vs NL-near: t(27) = 0.22, pholm = 0.828, d=0.02; BF10=0.20), highlighting the spatial specificity of learned suppression.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: Distractors evoked larger BOLD responses than neutral stimuli.
source: In addition, distractors evoked larger responses than neutral stimuli (t(27) = 4.67, pholm<0.001, d=0.10).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Differential BOLD responses to targets and distractors likely reflect a top-down modulation due to target relevance and a bottom-up effect of distractor salience.
source: These results likely reflect a top-down modulation due to target relevance and a bottom-up effect of distractor salience.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI data based on established attention theories.

claim: Neural populations with receptive fields corresponding to the HPDL showed significantly reduced BOLD responses compared to the diagonally opposite neutral location.
source: Neural populations with receptive fields corresponding to the HPDL showed significantly reduced BOLD responses compared to the diagonally opposite neutral location (NL-far; post hoc test HPDL vs NL-far: t(27) = 3.53, pholm = 0.003, d=0.59).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Suppression was not confined to the HPDL but also extended to close by neutral locations.
source: Intriguingly, and counter to the observed behavior, this suppression was not confined to the HPDL but also extended to close by neutral locations (NL-near vs NL-far: t(27) = 3.06, pholm = 0.007, d=0.51).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: BOLD responses between HPDL and NL-near locations did not reliably differ.
source: BOLD responses between HPDL and NL-near locations did not reliably differ (HPDL vs NL-near: t(27) = 0.47, pholm = 0.643, d=0.08; BF10=0.19).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data including Bayesian analysis.

claim: The pattern of neural suppression was present regardless of whether the distractor, target, or a neutral stimulus was presented at the HPDL and NL-near locations compared to NL-far.
source: This pattern of results was present regardless whether the distractor, target, or a neutral stimulus presented at the HPDL and NL-near locations compared to NL-far (6 of 6 paired t-tests: p<0.05; see table in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data across stimulus types.

claim: Neural suppression in early visual cortex had a less spatially selective (broader) pattern of suppression compared to the behavioral facilitation.
source: However, surprisingly neural suppression in EVC had a less spatially selective (i.e. broader) pattern of suppression compared to the behavioral facilitation, which was specific to the HPDL (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a comparison between the neural and behavioral results.

claim: BOLD responses corresponding to the HPDL were suppressed compared to the NL-far location during omission trials.
source: Crucially, BOLD responses corresponding to the HPDL were suppressed compared to the NL-far location (t(27) = 2.61, pholm = 0.024, d=0.45), as well as for the NL-near location compared to NL-far (t(27) = 2.82, pholm = 0.020, d=0.49).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data from omission trials.

claim: Neural responses at HPDL and NL-near did not reliably differ during omission trials.
source: Neural responses at HPDL and NL-near did not reliably differ (t(27) = 0.21, pholm = 0.835, d=0.04; BF10=0.21).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data from omission trials.

claim: The finding of suppression during omission trials suggests a proactive, or predictive, nature of distractor suppression in visual cortex.
source: This finding suggests a proactive, or predictive, nature of distractor suppression in visual cortex, activated merely by cues predicting the likely onset of a search display.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the omission trial fMRI data.

claim: Bayesian tests showed evidence for the absence of a difference in both accuracy and RTs across target locations.
source: Indeed, Bayesian tests showed evidence for the absence of a difference in both accuracy (NL-far vs NL-near: BF10=0.209, and NL-far vs HPDL: BF10=0.231) and RTs (NL-far vs NL-near: BF10=0.243, and NL-far vs HPDL: BF10=0.207).
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Behavioral results suggest that it is unlikely that increased attention toward the NL-far location explains the observed neural suppression pattern.
source: Therefore, in terms of both RT and response accuracy, behavioral results suggest that it is unlikely that increased attention toward the NL-far location explains the observed neural suppression pattern.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Only 35.7% of participants identified the correct HPDL in the post-experiment questionnaire.
source: At the group level, results indicated little knowledge of the statistical regularities with only 35.7% of participants identifying the correct HPDL.
evidence: This is based on questionnaire data collected after the experiment.

claim: There was no significant deviation from chance level (25%) in identifying the correct HPDL.
source: A chi-square goodness-of-fit test indicated no significant deviation from chance level of 25% (χ²(1, N = 28)=1.71, p=0.190; given that target and distractor stimuli appeared only at four locations, chance is arguably 25%), thus indicating that our results are unlikely to be explained by explicit attention strategies.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of questionnaire data.

claim: Results are unlikely to be explained by explicit attention strategies.
source: A chi-square goodness-of-fit test indicated no significant deviation from chance level of 25% (χ²(1, N = 28)=1.71, p=0.190; given that target and distractor stimuli appeared only at four locations, chance is arguably 25%), thus indicating that our results are unlikely to be explained by explicit attention strategies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the questionnaire data analysis.

claim: Results in the subsample of participants with incorrect HPDL responses were highly similar to the full sample results.
source: Critically, results were highly similar to Figure 4 in this subsample, providing strong evidence that distractor suppression in the present study does not reflect explicit attentional strategies.
evidence: This is supported by replication of the main fMRI analysis in a subsample shown in Figure 5.

claim: Distractor suppression in the present study does not reflect explicit attentional strategies.
source: Critically, results were highly similar to Figure 4 in this subsample, providing strong evidence that distractor suppression in the present study does not reflect explicit attentional strategies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the subsample analysis.

claim: The combined evidence favors an account emphasizing distractor contingencies learned by implicit visual statistical learning guiding subsequent visual search.
source: Instead, the combined evidence favors an account emphasizing distractor contingencies learned by implicit visual statistical learning guiding subsequent visual search, and that this implicit guide is spatially broad in EVC (affecting NL-near and HPDL similarly), as well as proactively deployed (evident also during omission trials).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence in the study.

claim: Results were qualitatively similar across small and medium ROI mask sizes.
source: Results were qualitatively similar across small and medium mask sizes, yielding significant simple main effects of location until very large mask sizes of 200 or more voxels per location, as expected by the predictable drop in location selectivity.
evidence: This is supported by control analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Results did not depend on the precise ROI mask size.
source: Thus, our results were not dependent on the precise ROI mask size supporting the reliability of our results.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the control analysis across different mask sizes.

claim: Results without normalization were qualitatively similar to the normalized results.
source: Results were qualitatively similar to the normalized results, suggesting that the normalization method did not introduce the observed results.
evidence: This is supported by control analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The normalization method did not introduce the observed results.
source: Results were qualitatively similar to the normalized results, suggesting that the normalization method did not introduce the observed results.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the control analysis comparing normalized and non-normalized data.

claim: Data support that early visual cortex is sensitive to statistical regularities.
source: In line with previous studies our data support that EVC is sensitive to statistical regularities (Adam and Serences, 2021; Beffara et al., 2023; Melloni et al., 2012; Richter et al., 2018; Richter and de Lange, 2019; Won et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022) highlighting that perception fundamentally relies on (implicit) priors (de Lange et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the current study's data and citations to previous research.

claim: Perception fundamentally relies on implicit priors.
source: In line with previous studies our data support that EVC is sensitive to statistical regularities (Adam and Serences, 2021; Beffara et al., 2023; Melloni et al., 2012; Richter et al., 2018; Richter and de Lange, 2019; Won et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022) highlighting that perception fundamentally relies on (implicit) priors (de Lange et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citation.

claim: Results extend previous studies on target learning to distractor suppression.
source: Our results extend previous studies on target learning (Beffara et al., 2023) to distractor suppression and show that EVC responses were suppressed at the HPDL and nearby neutral locations.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to previous research.

claim: Suppression was stimulus-unspecific, resulting in attenuated early visual cortex responses irrespective of the stimulus presented.
source: Suppression was stimulus-unspecific, resulting in attenuated EVC responses irrespective of the stimulus presented, complementing previous studies (Wang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by the current study's data and citations to previous research.

claim: Despite neural suppression of targets at HPDL, there were no behavioral costs for target identification at these locations.
source: However, despite this suppression we found no behavioral costs for target identification at these locations.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data showing no RT or accuracy differences for targets across locations.

claim: There is a discrepancy between the spatially broad neural suppression in early visual cortex and the more localized behavioral results.
source: Indeed, the discrepancy between the spatially broad neural suppression in EVC, extending beyond the HPDL to encompass neural populations coding for nearby neutral locations, and the more localized behavioral results, showing distractor suppression specific to the HPDL, further raises interesting questions about the relationship between neural activity in early visual areas and subsequent processing contributing to distractor suppression.
evidence: This is an observation comparing the neural and behavioral findings.

claim: Later processing stages in higher visual areas and downstream from visual cortex refine the initial neural suppression in early visual cortex to facilitate task performance.
source: Combined, these findings suggest that later processing stages in higher visual areas and downstream from visual cortex refine the initial neural suppression in EVC to facilitate task performance in a more nuanced fashion.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the discrepancy between neural and behavioral results.

claim: Areas in parietal and frontal cortex, including the dorsal attention network, may contribute to refinement of initial neural suppression.
source: It is plausible that areas in parietal and frontal cortex, including the dorsal attention network (Beffara et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022), contribute to this refinement.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous research cited.

claim: Suppression in early visual cortex does not merely reflect an epiphenomenon of the instantiation of spatial priority maps in later stages of cortical processing.
source: However, this does not mean that suppression in EVC merely reflects an epiphenomenon of the instantiation of spatial priority maps in later stages of cortical processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional role of EVC suppression.

claim: Early visual cortex may form an initial spatial bias that prioritizes a broad area of the visual field.
source: Instead, EVC may form an initial spatial bias that prioritizes a broad area of the visual field.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional role of EVC in distractor suppression.

claim: The initial spatial bias account seems well in line with the proactive nature of suppression.
source: This initial spatial bias account seems well in line with the proactive nature of suppression discussed in more detail later.
evidence: This is an inference connecting different aspects of the findings.

claim: Results fit well within the framework of spatial priority maps.
source: Overall, our results fit well within the framework of spatial priority maps (Awh et al., 2012; Bisley and Goldberg, 2010; Fecteau and Munoz, 2006; Itti and Koch, 2000; Serences and Yantis, 2006), de-emphasizing processing at and near the HPDL already at the earliest stages of the cortical visual hierarchy.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of existing theoretical frameworks.

claim: Spatial priority maps are frequently proposed to reside at the top of a hierarchy of topographic maps, with feature-specific maps at the bottom.
source: Spatial priority maps are frequently proposed to reside at the top of a hierarchy of topographic maps, with feature-specific maps at the bottom of this hierarchy of topographic maps (Fecteau and Munoz, 2006; Itti and Koch, 2000; Itti and Koch, 2001; Zelinsky and Bisley, 2015).
evidence: This describes an established theoretical framework supported by citations.

claim: The lack of stimulus specificity arises because spatial priority maps are implemented at a higher level than the feature-specific maps.
source: From this perspective, the lack of stimulus specificity arises because spatial priority maps are implemented at a higher level than the feature-specific maps.
evidence: This is an inference based on the hierarchical framework of priority maps.

claim: If priority signals from later processing stages are fed back into early sensory processing, the resulting modulations are necessarily stimulus-unspecific.
source: If priority signals from these later processing stages are then fed back into early sensory processing, the resulting modulations are necessarily stimulus-unspecific, as seen here.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation for the observed stimulus-unspecific suppression.

claim: The broad spatial suppression observed in early visual cortex fits well into the framework of spatial priority maps given wider receptive fields at later visual processing stages and reduced spatial acuity due to less spatially specific feedback signals.
source: Moreover, given the wider receptive fields at later visual processing stages and reduced spatial acuity due to less spatially specific feedback signals (Gilbert and Wiesel, 1989; Nassi and Callaway, 2009), the broad spatial suppression observed in EVC fits well into this framework.
evidence: This is an explanation for the broad suppression based on known properties of visual processing and feedback, supported by citations.

claim: Through statistical learning the weights within a spatial priority map are adjusted such that the location that more frequently contains a distractor is suppressed.
source: As argued above, we believe that through statistical learning the weights within a spatial priority map are adjusted such that the location that more frequently contains a distractor is suppressed (Theeuwes et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of how statistical learning affects priority maps, supported by citation.

claim: Suppression is instantiated before stimulus identification is completed.
source: Critically, the current findings indicate that this suppression is instantiated before stimulus identification is completed, suggesting that distractor suppression arises proactively.
evidence: This is an inference from the stimulus-unspecific nature of the suppression.

claim: Results from omission trials strongly support a proactive interpretation of distractor suppression.
source: Indeed, our results from omission trials strongly support such an interpretation.
evidence: This is supported by the omission trial fMRI data.

claim: The mere anticipation of search induced by the placeholder was sufficient to instantiate neural suppression.
source: Thus, the mere anticipation of search induced by the otherwise uninformative placeholder was sufficient to instantiate neural suppression.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the omission trial results.

claim: The proactive nature of neural suppression supports growing evidence for predictive and anticipatory processes in visual attention.
source: This proactive, or predictive, nature of neural suppression guided by implicit prior knowledge supports the growing evidence for predictive and anticipatory processes in visual attention (Beffara et al., 2023; Duncan et al., 2023; Serences et al., 2004; Zelinsky and Bisley, 2015).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to related research.

claim: The brain prepares for potential distractions based on learned probabilities.
source: In other words, the brain appears to prepare for potential distractions based on learned probabilities, reflecting a key aspect of predictive processing models.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of predictive processing.

claim: Results support a perspective of the visual system as relying on prediction to inform perception.
source: More fundamentally, our results support a perspective of the visual system as relying on prediction to inform perception (Clark, 2013; de Lange et al., 2018; Friston, 2005), echoing previous reports of selective pre-stimulus anticipatory activation in visual cortex (Kok et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations to predictive processing frameworks.

claim: Attention enhances BOLD responses in visual cortex.
source: It is well established that attention enhances BOLD responses in visual cortex (Maunsell, 2015; Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004; Williford and Maunsell, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: There was no behavioral facilitation for target stimuli presented at the far neutral location.
source: First, there was no behavioral facilitation for target stimuli presented at the far neutral location, contrary to what one might expect if participants employed an explicit strategy.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Control analysis excluding participants who indicated the correct HPDL yielded qualitatively identical results to the full sample.
source: Thus, we performed a control analysis that excluded all participants that indicated the correct HPDL location in the questionnaire, thereby possibly expressing explicit awareness of the contingencies. This control analysis yielded qualitatively identical results to the full sample, showing significant distractor suppression in EVC.
evidence: This is supported by the control analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: It is unlikely that explicit attentional strategies drive the observed results.
source: Therefore, it is unlikely that explicit attentional strategies, and the enhancement of locations far from the HPDL, drive the results observed here.
evidence: This is an inference from the control analyses and questionnaire data.

claim: Current findings are consistent with an account emphasizing the automatic deployment of spatial priors based on implicitly learned statistical regularities.
source: Instead, the current findings are consistent with an account emphasizing the automatic deployment of spatial priors (He et al., 2022) based on implicitly learned statistical regularities.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citation.

claim: This account echoes the crucial role of implicit statistical learning.
source: This account echoes the crucial role of implicit statistical learning (Kim et al., 2009; Turk-Browne et al., 2009; Turk-Browne et al., 2010), adjusting the weights within the proposed spatial priority landscape (Theeuwes et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Repetition suppression and stimulus adaptation must be differentiated from the effects of statistical learning investigated in this study.
source: Repetition suppression (Henson, 2016; Summerfield et al., 2008; Todorovic and de Lange, 2012) and stimulus adaptation (Adam and Serences, 2021) must be differentiated from the effects of statistical learning investigated here.
evidence: This is a conceptual distinction supported by citations.

claim: Stimulus features (orientation and color) were randomized across trials and not related to the key location manipulation.
source: Crucially, in the present study, stimulus features (orientation and color) were randomized across trials and not related to the key location manipulation.
evidence: This describes a key aspect of the experimental design.

claim: Simple adaptation cannot account for the observed results.
source: Thus, simple adaptation cannot account for the observed results.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental design.

claim: Early visual cortex is mostly tuned to simple stimulus features, such as orientation.
source: First, we report suppression of neural populations in EVC, which is mostly tuned to simple stimulus features, such as orientation (Hubel and Wiesel, 1962), which do not repeat more often at the HPDL.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EVC function supported by citation.

claim: Suppression was observed irrespective of the stimulus type, including target stimuli which were equiprobable at all locations.
source: Second, we observed suppression irrespective of the stimulus type, including target stimuli, which were equiprobable at all locations, and for neutral stimuli, which were in fact less likely to occur at the HPDL.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis.

claim: During omission trials no stimuli were presented at all, but similar location-specific suppression was observed.
source: Finally, during omission trials no stimuli were presented at all, but similar location-specific suppression was observed.
evidence: This is supported by the omission trial fMRI data.

claim: Combined factors rule out an account along the lines of repetition suppression.
source: Combined these factors rule out an account along the lines of repetition suppression.
evidence: This is an inference from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The observed BOLD suppression is unlikely to be driven by priming and is instead more consistent with statistical learning.
source: This indicates that the observed BOLD suppression is unlikely to be driven by priming and is instead more consistent with statistical learning.
evidence: This is an inference from the priming control analysis.

claim: Modulations in early visual cortex may reflect a consequence of downstream instantiations of priority maps feeding back into early visual cortex.
source: It is conceivable that our results reflect a consequence of downstream instantiations of priority maps, in higher visual areas or beyond, feeding back into EVC; e.g., possibly from parietal cortex (Bisley and Goldberg, 2010; Zelinsky and Bisley, 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the source of EVC modulations, supported by citations.

claim: Data is also consistent with the notion that early visual cortex itself stores the relevant spatial priority maps.
source: Alternatively, our data is also consistent with the notion that EVC itself stores the relevant spatial priority maps, e.g., by short-term synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis about the source of EVC modulations.

claim: Given the high spatial acuity of early visual cortex representations, it would be surprising if priority maps represented in early visual cortex have the broad spatial characteristics observed.
source: However, given the high spatial acuity of EVC representations, it would be surprising if priority maps represented in EVC have the broad spatial characteristics as observed here.
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of EVC.

claim: Data provide tentative evidence that modulations in early visual cortex due to learned distractor suppression are potentially a consequence of downstream instantiated priority maps.
source: Thus, while future research is required to address this question in more detail, our data provide tentative evidence that modulations in EVC, due to learned distractor suppression, are potentially a consequence of downstream instantiated priority maps.
evidence: This is a tentative conclusion based on inference from the data.

claim: An exploratory analysis suggests that distractor suppression may show different patterns in V1 compared to V2.
source: However, an exploratory analysis suggests that distractor suppression may show different patterns in V1 compared to V2 (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is based on exploratory analysis presented in Appendix 1.

claim: Results in V2 mirrored those reported for the combined early visual cortex ROI.
source: In brief, results in V2 mirrored those reported for the combined EVC ROI (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on exploratory analysis comparing V1 and V2.

claim: Results in V1 appeared to be only partially modulated by distractor contingencies.
source: In contrast, results in V1 appeared to be only partially modulated by distractor contingencies, and if so, the modulation was less robust and not as spatially broad as in V2.
evidence: This is based on exploratory analysis of V1 and V2.

claim: The study design did not optimize the delineation of early visual areas.
source: First, our design did not optimize the delineation of early visual areas (e.g. no functional retinotopy), limiting the accuracy of V1 and V2 segmentation.
evidence: This is a limitation of the study design.

claim: Analyses were conducted in volumetric space, which reduces spatial precision.
source: Additionally, analyses were conducted in volumetric space, which further reduces spatial precision.
evidence: This is a limitation of the analysis approach.

claim: It is possible to estimate unique contributions of omission trials to the BOLD signal given the experimental design.
source: First, as omission trials were randomly intermixed with search trials, separated by variable ITIs, and modeled as separate regressors, it is possible to well estimate unique contributions of the omission trials to the BOLD signal.
evidence: This is an explanation of the validity of the analysis approach.

claim: The parameter estimates for omission trials were close to zero (implicit baseline, no visual stimulation).
source: Indeed, the parameter estimates for omission trials were close to zero (i.e. implicit baseline, no visual stimulation), supporting the validity of our inference.
evidence: This is supported by the omission trial fMRI data.

claim: A prediction error should be uniform across the search display if neural activation during omission trials reflects prediction error.
source: The prediction of a stimulus appearing is equally violated for all locations; hence, we believe that a prediction error should be uniform across the search display.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be expected under a prediction error account.

claim: It seems unlikely that surprise related to the omission of the search display can account for the present results.
source: Thus, it seems unlikely that surprise related to the omission of the search display itself can account for the present results.
evidence: This is an inference ruling out an alternative explanation.

claim: The present data do not elucidate whether suppression is preceded by a brief attentional enhancement of the HPDL.
source: Finally, due to the limited temporal resolution of BOLD data, the present data do not elucidate whether the present suppression is preceded by a brief attentional enhancement of the HPDL, as implied by some prior work (Huang et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a limitation of the fMRI method acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Even if suppression is preceded by transient enhancement, this would still constitute proactive distractor suppression as the suppression would arise before search onset.
source: Critically, we believe that this variation would nonetheless constitute proactive distractor suppression as the suppression would still arise before search onset.
evidence: This is a clarification of the interpretation of proactive suppression.

claim: Findings elucidate that distractor suppression is a multifaceted process involving both broad, proactive neural mechanisms within the early visual system and more focused downstream modulations.
source: Our findings elucidate that distractor suppression is a multifaceted process involving both broad, proactive neural mechanisms within the early visual system and more focused downstream modulations.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: The broad suppression in early visual cortex may serve as an initial filter or bias, which is then fine-tuned by higher cognitive processes downstream.
source: The broad suppression in EVC may serve as an initial filter or bias, which is then fine-tuned by higher (cognitive) processes downstream.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional role of EVC suppression.

claim: Results indicate that the brain's predictive mechanisms, informed by statistical learning, do not always manifest with spatial precision but can exhibit a broader scope.
source: Thereby our results indicate that the brain's predictive mechanisms, informed by statistical learning, do not always manifest with spatial precision but can exhibit a broader scope.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The broad suppression could represent a neural efficiency trade-off, where the brain balances the cost of precise suppression against the resulting benefits for attentional control.
source: This phenomenon could represent a neural efficiency trade-off, where the brain balances the cost of precise suppression against the resulting benefits for attentional control.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the broad suppression.

claim: Feedback mechanisms signaling spatial priority maps from higher-level to lower-level visual areas could lack the spatial acuity to effectuate more precise location-specific suppression in early visual cortex.
source: Alternatively, feedback mechanisms, which may signal the hypothesized spatial priority maps from higher-level to lower-level visual areas, could lack the spatial acuity to effectuate more precise location-specific suppression in EVC.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative explanation for the broad suppression.

claim: The finding that suppression is detectable during omission trials strongly supports the proactive nature of the deployment of spatial priority maps in guiding visual search.
source: Our pivotal finding, that suppression is detectable even during omission trials, strongly supports the proactive nature of the deployment of spatial priority maps in guiding visual search, as also suggested by recent behavioral studies (Huang et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2022; Kong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a key conclusion supported by the omission trial data and citations to related behavioral studies.

claim: The broad, proactive nature of neural suppression, alongside its stimulus-unspecific characteristics, suggests a complex interplay between low-level visual processing and higher-order cognitive functions in attentional control.
source: In sum, the broad, proactive nature of neural suppression, alongside its stimulus-unspecific characteristics, suggests a complex interplay between low-level visual processing and higher-order cognitive functions in attentional control to shape spatial priority maps underlying visual search.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings.

claim: Results underscore the significant role of statistical learning and predictive processing in modulating neural responses within the visual cortex.
source: Finally, our results underscore the significant role of statistical learning and predictive processing in modulating neural responses within the visual cortex, thereby facilitating efficient visual processing amidst the plethora of distracting stimuli impinging upon our senses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: MRI data was acquired from 32 human volunteers.
source: We acquired MRI data from 32 human volunteers.
evidence: This describes the sample size for data acquisition.

claim: Data from one participant was lost due to technical problems.
source: Data from one participant was lost due to technical problems.
evidence: This describes data loss.

claim: Data from three participants were excluded from analysis due to excessive motion during MRI scanning.
source: Data from three participants were excluded from analysis due to excessive motion during MRI scanning, defined as an average framewise displacement exceeding 2 SD above the group median.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria and number of excluded participants.

claim: The final sample size was n=28.
source: Data from the remaining participants were analyzed, resulting in a final sample size of n=28, satisfying our a priori defined minimum required sample size of n ≥ 24 (based on an a priori power calculation to obtain a power of 80% to detect an effect size Cohen's d=0.5 at a default alpha = 0.05).
evidence: This describes the final analyzed sample size.

claim: All participants included in the data analysis showed reliable task performance.
source: All participants included in the data analysis showed reliable task performance, evident as each subject's response accuracy >82% (group mean 93%) and mean RT for each participant <1050 ms (all trials; group mean 858 ms).
evidence: This describes the performance criteria for included participants.

claim: The study was approved by the local ethics committee (Vaste Commissie Wetenschap en Ethiek of the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam: VCWE-2021-208R1).
source: The study followed institutional guidelines and was approved by the local ethics committee (Vaste Commissie Wetenschap en Ethiek of the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam: VCWE-2021-208R1).
evidence: This describes ethical approval for the study.

claim: Written informed consent and MRI compatibility screening was obtained before study participation.
source: Written informed consent and MRI compatibility screening was obtained before study participation.
evidence: This describes the consent process.

claim: Participants were compensated 15€/hr.
source: Participants were compensated 15€/hr and were fully debriefed after completion of the experiment.
evidence: This describes participant compensation.
